text:
Court of Queen
’
s Bench of Alberta

Citation: Nasin v. Nasin, 2008 ABQB 219

Date:

20080407

Docket:

4803 139361

Registry:

Edmonton

Between:

Shoaib Ahmad Nasin

Plaintiff

-
and -

Yegana Nasin

Defendant

Corrected judgment:
A corrigendum was issued on June 6, 2008; the
corrections have been made to the text and the corrigendum is appended to
this judgment.

_______________________________________________________

Reasons for Judgment

of
the

Honourable Madam Justice A.B. Moen

_______________________________________________________

Introduction

[
1
]

Shoaib and Yegana Nasin were
married for a very short time
–
just short of
nine months. They were married on July 9, 2005 and separated April 2, 2006.
There are no children.

[
2
]

They were married according to
Muslim tradition and culture. During the time of their marriage they
accumulated property the division of which is the subject of this trial. They
disagree about what comprises the matrimonial property, what exemptions apply and
how it should be divided. In particular, the evidence disclosed that there were
a number of Muslim traditions concerning payment for events leading up to the
marriage.

[
3
]

Further, according to Muslim
tradition, just before the marriage ceremony took place, they entered into a
form of pre‑nuptial agreement called the Mahr in which Mr. Nasin agreed
to pay Mrs. Nasin $10,000.00 in the event of the failure of their marriage. Mr.
Nasin maintains that this forms part of the matrimonial property and is not a
separate contract. Mrs. Nasin disagrees.

[
4
]

The issues arising in this case
are:

1.          Is the Mahr a separate contract relating
to matrimonial property that ought to be enforced by the courts?

2.          What
is the matrimonial property to be divided?

3.          Are
either of the parties entitled to any exemptions from this property?

4.          How
should the property be divided justly?

Discussion

[
5
]

This couple had some property that
accrued in value during their very short marriage. I must determine what that
property is and how it should be divided. I must also consider a bargain made
before the marriage as to what the husband would pay the wife in the event of a
divorce. This bargain was called a Mahr.

A.       Is the Mahr
enforceable?

1.
Is the Mahr a separate contract
relating to matrimonial property that ought to be enforced by the courts?

[
6
]

Just before the marriage took
place, in this Muslim tradition as explained to me at the trial, the bride and
groom bargain as to an amount that he will pay in the event of a marriage
breakdown. In this particular case, the parties each chose an uncle to
negotiate on their behalf. Those uncles left the wedding to have a discussion.
They returned and suggested that the amount should be determined by the future
husband. Mr. Nasin said that he was offering $10,000.00. She said that she was
worth a million dollars but accepted the offer of $10,000.00. Once that bargain
was made, the wedding proceeded.

[
7
]

There was no written contract
about the Mahr between the parties although the ceremony was, apparently, video
taped. That tape was not put into evidence. However, from the evidence before
me, I find that there was a contract: there was an offer, an acceptance and
consideration. I would characterize the contract as a pre‑nuptial
agreement.

[
8
]

The husband acknowledges that he
has an obligation under religious law. But he suggests that it is a religious
obligation that should not be considered or enforced by the Courts.

[
9
]

He says that he did not agree to
pay the Mahr amount in addition to the obligations under the Act, noting three
British Columbia cases where the Mahr agreements were in writing and expressly
indicated that the Mahr amount was in addition to the obligations under the
law:
Nathoo v. Nathoo
,
[1996] B.C.J. No. 2720 (B.C.S.C.)
;
Amlani
v. Hirani
,
2000 BCSC 1653
,
[2000] B.C.J. No. 2357
; and
N.M.M. v.
N.S.M.
,
2004 BCSC 346
,
[2004] B.C.J. No. 642
.

[
10
]

Mr. Nasin further argues that if
the Court does consider the agreement to be a contract the following should be
considered:

a.          The agreement was not in writing and there
was no testimony from either party to indicate whether they meant that the Mahr
amount was to be in addition to, and not in substitution for, his obligations
under the law.

b.          It would not make sense to suggest that
the Mahr will always be in addition to the rights under the local jurisdiction
since the Mahr could be more than the total value of property owned by the
parties at the date of the divorce leading to a conflict between the
matrimonial property regime and the Mahr.

c.          It makes more sense to consider the Mahr
as one of the factors under
s. 8
of the
Matrimonial Property Act
‑
"the terms of an oral or written agreement between the spouses".

[
11
]

Canadian courts have been divided
on the enforcement of the Mahr. British Columbia courts in the above three
cases found that a Mahr was enforceable. However, in Ontario, in
Kaddoura
v. Hammoud
,
[1998] O.J. No. 5054
, Rutherford J. (at paras. 25‑26)
held that the Court would not, and should not, determine the rights and
obligations of the parties under the Mahr, as it would lead the Court into the
"religious thicket".
Khan v. Khan
,
2005 ONCJ 155
,

[2005] O.J. No. 1923
dealt with a "Nikah"
–
a marriage agreement recognized in Pakistan.
In
Khan

the Nikah signed by the parties waived any entitlement to support upon
separation. Clark J. was prepared to enter the "religious thicket" to
hold that the Nikah bound the parties civilly, but concluded that the waiver of
any entitlement to support should be set aside because the wife did not
understand the nature and consequences of such a marriage agreement.

[
12
]

The Supreme Court of Canada in
Bruker
v. Marcovitz
,
2007 SCC 54 (CanLII)
,
[2007] S.C.J. No. 54
, has recently addressed the question
of the enforceability of religious agreements. The parties, a Jewish couple,
entered into a Consent to Corollary Relief, in which they agreed that they
would attend before a rabbinical court to obtain a get‑ a Jewish
religious divorce. The husband refused to comply, alleging that the agreement
was not a valid contractual obligation under Quebec law and that his freedom of
religion under the
Quebec
Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms
would be
infringed if the agreement was civilly enforced.

[
13
]

Abella J. for the majority held
that the fact that a dispute has a religious aspect does not make it non‑justiciable.
Persons can transfer their moral obligations into legally binding ones.
Therefore, the promises in such an agreement must be considered to determine
whether they are valid and binding under the relevant law. Here, that law is
the
Matrimonial Property Act
.

[
14
]

I have found that the Mahr in this
case is a contract. While it was not in writing, it was an exchange of promises
intended by the parties to be binding. The husband argues that there is
uncertainty in the contract as to whether he meant that he would pay at least
$10,000.00 and that it should be included in the matrimonial property
settlement. There is not a shred of evidence around the making of the Mahr that
would suggest that this was in his mind at the time. He and his soon-to-be wife
made a bargain. It was a pre‑nuptial agreement which must be addressed
under the
Matrimonial Property Act
.

[
15
]

Years ago, by public policy,
parties could not enter into pre‑nuptial agreements that would be
enforced by the courts. Usually, the name on the title was that of the husband
and the wife had no legal right to share in the property. The courts eventually
decided that a woman who had put her life and energy into the property was not
to be left with nothing if the marriage or relationship dissolved.

[
16
]

Then the legislatures in Canada
enacted matrimonial property legislation.  In Alberta that legislation
addresses contracts made before marriage as well as those made while a couple
are separating. The main part of the
Alberta
Matrimonial Property Act
‑
Part I ‑ deals with how property is to be divided in the event of a
divorce. However, in Part III of the Act, the legislature is clear that the
principles set out in Part I do not apply when there is "a subsisting
written agreement with each other that is enforceable under section 38 and that
provides for the status, ownership and division of that property.": s.
37(1).

[
17
]

The Act provides at s. 37(2) that
"An agreement under subsection (1) may be entered into by 2 persons in
contemplation of their marriage to each other but is unenforceable until after
the marriage." Here the Mahr was made before the marriage and the marriage
is now over. The Mahr falls under s. 37(2) of the Act.

[
18
]

However, the Act also provides
that certain formalities must be met when such an agreement is made in
contemplation of marriage. Those formalities are set out in s. 38 of the Act
and are the same formalities as those required for a Separation Agreement under
Part I of the Act:

38(1)
... each person,..., has acknowledged, in writing, apart from the other spouse
or person

(a)
that the spouse or person is aware of the nature and the effect of the
agreement,

(b)
that the spouse or person is aware of the possible future claims to property
the spouse or person may have under this Act and that the spouse or person
intends to give up these claims to the extent necessary to give effect to the
agreement, and

(c)
that the spouse or person is executing the agreement freely and voluntarily
without any compulsion on the part of the other spouse or person.

[
19
]

Further, the acknowledgement must
be made before a lawyer other than the lawyer acting for the other spouse or
person or before whom the acknowledgement is made by the other spouse or
person.

[
20
]

These are mandatory under the Act
before a pre‑nuptial agreement will be enforced by the courts.  As a
matter of public policy as set out in the legislation, parties entering into
marriage may enter into an agreement with respect to the division of their
property if their marriage fails.  However, that agreement will not be enforced
by the courts unless the requirements set out in the Act are met.

[
21
]

There are good reasons for this
policy. Where there is an unequal balance of power between the future husband
and wife, the courts must be satisfied that the woman or man entered into the
marriage of their own free will, knowing that they have property rights but
willingly giving up those rights. The courts enforce the requirements so as to
ensure that the policy established by the legislature is maintained.

[
22
]

Here, we have a pre‑nuptial
agreement that met none of the requirements. It was not in writing. There was
no certificate of acknowledgment that met the requirements of s. 38 of the Act.
The parties did not receive independent legal advice.

[
23
]

Therefore, even though the Mahr is
a pre‑nuptial contract, it is unenforceable.

[
24
]

As to the religious aspects fo the
Mahr, if parties enter into pre-nuptial agreements in a religious context, they
will be enforced if they meet the requirements under the
Matrimonial
Property Act
and the courts do not find the contracts invalid for other
reasons.

[
25
]

Therefore, this couple, like all
couples in Alberta, must divide their property in accordance with Part 1 of the

Matrimonial Property Act
.

B.       Division of
Matrimonial Property

[
26
]

The leading case on the proper
date for the valuation and division of matrimonial property under the
Matrimonial
Property Act
is
Hodgson v. Hodgson
,
2005 ABCA 13
,
[2005] A.J.
No. 22
.
The Alberta Court of Appeal in
Hodgson
held that the
proper date for the valuation and division of matrimonial property is the date
of trial.

[
27
]

In this case, not all of the
valuations were made as at trial and some of the property was not properly
valued. However, I will attempt to find values as at trial and then will
determine the appropriate division of that property.

[
28
]

The Court of Appeal
in
Hodgson

described the four‑step process for the division of matrimonial property
that is set out by
sections 7
and
8
of the
Matrimonial Property Act

(paras. 18‑22):

1.          Determine
all property owned at the date of trial;

2.          Discern the property that is exempt from
distribution under section 7(2). The exempt property under section 7(2) is
valued at the date of acquisition or the date of marriage.

3.          Determine what property falls under
section 7(3), which is then distributed between the parties in a manner that is
just and equitable taking into consideration the factors set out in
section 8
.

4.          Divide the balance of the remaining
property valued at the date of trial equally, unless it would be unjust and
inequitable to do so considering the factors set out in
section 8
.

[
29
]

First, we must determine what the
matrimonial property is and what its value is at the date of the trial. Then we
must determine if there are any exemptions associated with that property. Then
we must determine if there should be an equal division of the property arising
from the exempt property. Finally, we must determine if there should be an
uneven division of any property acquired during the marriage.

1.

What is the matrimonial property to be
divided?

[
30
]

The house is not in joint names.
However, the division of matrimonial property in Alberta does not rely on whose
names are on the property. In this case, there is property arising from exempt
property that the parties brought into the marriage and there was property and
debt acquired during the marriage. The law requires that I look at the property
accrued from exempt property differently than the property acquired during the
marriage.

[
31
]

In the case before me, the
potential matrimonial property comprises a house, a business
–
Y & S Event Decor and the assets of that
business, RRSPs, stock options, household furnishings, an automobile and debt.
The discussion on debt also involves a discussion on wedding costs.

a)       The
house

[
32
]

Matrimonial home is defined in the

Matrimonial Property Act
, R.S.A 2000, c. M‑8 as amended, as
property that is owned by one or both spouses and that has been occupied by the
spouses as their family home. The house here falls under that definition as it
was the only home that was occupied by Mr. and Ms. Nasin during their marriage
and it was and is owned by Mr. Nasin. Therefore,
prima face
, the house
in question here is matrimonial property.

[
33
]

The house was bought after the
engagement and before the marriage by the husband. He paid a down payment.
Prior to the marriage, the wife had some input as to the house to be purchased
and as to the finishes in the home but paid nothing towards the purchase of the
home.

[
34
]

The husband paid $234,048.00 (plus
change orders) for the house and financed it with a down payment of $12,145.00
and a mortgage of $239,235.41. There was some oral evidence by the husband that
his mother contributed to the down payment. However, neither the title to the
house nor the loan documents had her name on them. I am, therefore, ignoring
any contribution that she may have made as that is between her and her son.

[
35
]

The value of the house at the date
of the marriage is agreed by the parties to be $265,000.00. Unfortunately, I
was given no balance for the mortgage on the date of the marriage. Therefore, I
am using the amount of the original mortgage which had been paid down very
little before the marriage but with no evidence, I cannot guess as to the
amount of the mortgage at the date of the wedding. I find that the equity in
the house at the date of the marriage was $25,765.00. This amount includes the
down payment.

[
36
]

The husband took possession of the
house on June 6, 2005. The couple were married on July 9, 2005 and the wife
moved in two months later when she obtained a job in Edmonton, having come from
Calgary.

[
37
]

There were two experts called to
give evidence regarding the value of the house at the date of separation. The
parties tried to devalue each other's appraiser.

[
38
]

The husband's appraiser gave the
value of the home at the date of marriage, the date of separation and the date
of trial. The wife's appraiser gave a value of the house as of August 15, 2007,
shortly before trial.

[
39
]

It was suggested by the wife that
the husband's appraiser was not qualified to do the appraisal because he had
lost his designation and then regained it. He completed one of the appraisals
while he was not designated. That appraisal was properly co‑signed by a
qualified appraiser. The only expert evidence I have about the value of the
house for two important periods ‑ at the time of trial and at the time of
separation ‑ comes from the husband's appraiser. I note that the wife
accepts the husband's appraisal for the value of the home at the date of the
marriage. I accept the husband's appraiser's evidence where I have no other
evidence and I compromise his evidence where there are two expert appraisals.

[
40
]

The husband's appraisal as at
April 2, 2006 (the date of separation) was $312,000.00.

[
41
]

The husband's expert gave a value
for the house as of February 17, 2007 as $425,000.00 and as of September 5,
2007 at $450,000.00. The wife's expert gave a value of $505,000.00 as of August
15, 2007. They both looked at recent sales in the area and both attempted to
come up with a value compared to those sales.

[
42
]

I am not an expert in this area
and both experts who gave evidence at trial gave pros and cons for the value
that they gave the house, and they both admitted that valuing a house is in
part a science and in part art. Further there were pros and cons with respect
to the expertise of each of the appraisers. Therefore, given I cannot pick
apart the valuations with any degree of certainty, I will select a value as of
the date of trial about half way between those two values ($450,000.00 and
$505,000.00), that is $475,000.00 for the value of the home at the date of the
trial.

[
43
]

The increase in the value of the
house is characterized as matrimonial property arising from exempt property and
must be treated under
s. 7(3)
of the
Matrimonial Property Act
.          That
increase in value to the date of trial is $210,000.00.

b)       The
wife's automobile

[
44
]

The wife came into the marriage
with a vehicle purchased before the wedding and she still has possession. Both
agree that it is exempt and there is no increase in value. It will not be
included in matrimonial property.

c)       Stock
options

[
45
]

The husband's stock options in the
company for which he worked had decreased in value by the time of trial. The
wife submits that they should be retained by the husband, and that the loss
cannot be counted as a liability:
Harrower v. Harrower
,
1989 CanLII 221 (AB CA)
,
[1989]
A.J. No. 629 (C.A.)
and
Stewart v. Stewart
,
1992 CanLII 14150 (AB QB)
,
[1992] A.J. No. 531
(Q.B.)
. I agree. The husband retains the stock options and they will not form
part of the matrimonial property.

d)       RRSPs

[
46
]

At the date of the marriage the
husband had RRSPs worth $5,425.00, and the wife had $852.00. By the date of
trial, the husband's RRSPs increased in value by $4,966.99; the wife's by
$188.00 for a total increase of $5,154.99. The increase in RRSPs is matrimonial
property which must be treated under
s. 7(3)
.

e)       Household
furnishings

[
47
]

The husband purchased a TV and
appliances shortly before the wedding, but paid for them after. The wife
submits that although the original purchase price for these items was $6,800.00,
their present value of $3,900.00 should be divided equally, in part, because he
paid for them after the wedding. The husband said that he paid for them out of
the proceeds of the business. The husband argues that the appliances are part
of the value of the house, and that the wife took some property from the house
that has not been accounted for. Further, he argues there is no evidentiary
basis for placing a value at trial on the two year old TV and appliances.

[
48
]

I note that the appraisals for the
house list the vacuum and dishwasher (built‑ins), but no other
appliances. Therefore, the TV and appliances do not form part of the value for
the house but form part of the value for matrimonial property. The husband is
quite correct that I do not have any evidence as to the value of those items at
trial, save for the original purchase price. Household furnishings tend to
depreciate rather quickly. He had the use of those items during the marriage
and from the date of the separation to the date of the trial, given that he
still lives in the house.

[
49
]

The wife when she left took
kitchen things and bathroom things and her clothing. The kitchen and bathroom
things were gifts from her family. She left everything else.

[
50
]

I find that there is value in the
furnishings and that the wife is entitled to share in the value because they
were purchased with matrimonial funds. Therefore I value the furnishings at
$3,000.00 at trial for the purpose of division of matrimonial property.

[
51
]

This is property that must be
divided under
s. 7(4)
of the
Matrimonial Property Act
.

f)        Y.
& S. Event Decor

[
52
]

Prior to the wedding, the parties
discussed going into business using materials purchased for the wedding as an
investment in a wedding decorating business. They would use the decorations for
their wedding and then use them in the business. Prior to the wedding, the
husband bought decorations for the wedding. All the ordered materials were not
received in time for the wedding. When they arrived after the wedding, the
parties put those materials into the business. That business folded when the
parties separated.

[
53
]

There are no receipts put into
evidence to establish the value of the materials purchased by the husband and
by the company during the marriage, nor evidence of the value of those
materials after separation. The parties appear to agree that the materials are
worth $29,000.00 as at the date of trial. Nothing has happened to those
materials since the separation. The husband suggests that the wife should buy
the materials for $25,000.00 or the parties should sell the materials for a
price to be agreed. Given that these parties are probably incapable of agreeing
on a selling price and a division of that selling price, I am deeming those
goods to be worth $29,000.00 at the date of trial and at the date of
separation. I discuss exemptions later.

[
54
]

I also find that there is no good
will value in the company to be divided. The company is defunct. It was not a
going concern after the separation. There was no expert evidence given at trial
in any event.

[
55
]

The wife claims that Y & S
Event Decor lost $7,000.00 in contracts. After the marital breakdown she says
that she offered to complete the contracts but the husband refused to allow her
to access the materials needed to do so. She also said that she assigned the
contracts to a third party to avoid potential legal exposure for breach of
contract. There have been no lawsuits. She argues that the husband should
account for that loss on the basis of dissipation. "Dissipation is another
word for waste. ...  to show dissipation there must be an element of bad faith
or neglect.":
Metz v. Metz

(2004),
34 Alta. L.R. (4th) 252

at para.
37
,
2004 ABQB 528
.

[
56
]

In cases of dissipation, there may
be an unequal distribution of property ordered or the amount of dissipation
found may be included in the property to be distributed. See
Wright‑Watts
v. Watts
,
2005 ABQB 708
at para.
57
;
Tocker v. Tocker

(2000),
273 A.R. 257
at para.
77
,
2000 ABQB 582
; and
Potter v. Potter

(2001),
300 A.R. 124
at para.
89
,
2001 ABQB 810
.

[
57
]

In this case, the evidence does
not support that the husband dissipated the property of the company. It is true
that there were contracts that the husband and wife did not finish. This was
all part of the acrimony involved in the separation. In any event, there was no
valuation of those contracts and if I were to value them I would be guessing.
The circumstances in this case do not warrant an unequal division of
matrimonial property based on dissipation. Finally, I question whether the
unfulfilled contracts may be characterized as matrimonial property.

[
58
]

Aside from any exemption allowed
for the material purchased by the husband before the marriage, this is matrimonial
property to be divided pursuant to
s. 7(4)
of the
Matrimonial Property Act
.
There were materials purchased during the marriage and contracts fulfilled
during the marriage.

[
59
]

Finally, I discuss the debts
relating to the business below.

g)       Other
property

[
60
]

While they were married, the wife
received a settlement in the amount of $13,000.00 for an accident that happened
before the marriage. She paid her mother $10,000.00 to defray the costs of the
pre‑wedding parties. The other $3,000.00 was used by her to pay down her
Visa.

[
61
]

The parties received $14,000.00 in
cash as wedding gifts.  The husband used it to pay some of his debts from
before the wedding without the wife's authorization. Because the husband used
the money to pay his debts, this was not an asset in existence at the date of
trial. The wife says that the husband should account to her for her half of the
money gifts. The husband says that the cash gifts were given to him by his
friends and family to help defray the costs of the wedding, but there was no
corroborating evidence.  The husband acknowledges that some of the money gifts
were to the wife. There is no accounting as to who gave the gifts and how much.

[
62
]

I find that the husband must
account for the $14,000.00 in cash wedding gifts as matrimonial property under
s. 7(4) of the Act.

[
63
]

The parties also have a dispute as
to the property acquired by each of them before the wedding as part of the
traditions associated with their culture. The wife received gifts of jewellery
from her friends and family before the wedding. There were also debts incurred
by each of them. Their disputes were not enlightened by expert evidence as to
how these traditions usually work. Neither of the parties brought an expert in
their traditions to give expert evidence about Muslim traditions in Afghanistan
from which their families originated.

[
64
]

The husband and wife agreed that
the husband was to bear the costs of the wedding and that by tradition, the
bride carried the costs of the engagement party.

[
65
]

The husband suggests that I should
account for the costs of the engagement party and his contribution to it. In
written argument the husband asserts that he paid her $4,000.00 toward the
engagement party cost, although this is disputed by the wife. I note, however,
that his evidence at trial was that he gave her the money as a gift following
the engagement party when she visited his family in Edmonton. He indicated that
in his culture, he was expected to give her an engagement gift of cash. The
wife's evidence was she paid for the engagement party, and that the $4,000.00
was an engagement gift given after the engagement.

[
66
]

There were also issues as to the
costs of the wedding which the husband traditionally would pay for. According
to the husband, the wedding cost much more than he anticipated. He gave
evidence that he had a target of $35,000 in mind but that the wedding cost
$50,000.00 to $60,000.00. He says that he paid for the wedding from his
savings, from the sale of his car ($11,000.00) and with the help of his
parents. There was some disagreement between the parties as to why the wedding
went over the husband's budget and the wife stated in her evidence that she did
not know that there was such a budget. Whatever happened, it was prior to the
actual marriage and I find that the husband is responsible for the costs of the
wedding according to their custom.

[
67
]

The wife acknowledged that prior
to the wedding she also received gifts of jewellery as part of the tradition.
There was no valuation of the jewellery, nor was there even a list. Because
these were gifts given prior to the wedding, they are the wife's. All gifts
given prior to the wedding are the property of the person who received them.

[
68
]

Because these expenditures were
prior to the wedding, and the jewellery was given before the wedding, they do
not form matrimonial debt, nor do the pre‑nuptial gifts form matrimonial
property and I do not take them into account.

[
69
]

Therefore, except for the amount
to be credited against the value of the materials in the company as discussed
below, each party must bear whatever costs they incurred with respect to the
pre‑wedding events and gifts and none of the costs nor the value will be
included as matrimonial property.

h)       Debts

[
70
]

Both of the parties had debt when
they came into the marriage.

[
71
]

The husband argues that the line
of credit and the Visa charges were related to the wedding costs and their
living expenses and therefore no deduction should be made for the amount he owed
at the time of the marriage, that is, the wife should share the debt he
incurred before the wedding. The wife says that the amount of debt that should
be accounted for in the calculation of matrimonial property should be that
incurred during the marriage, that is, the husband was responsible for the
expenses relating to the wedding and therefore those expenses should not be
counted. Further, the wife disputes the purpose of the expenditures made by the
husband just before the wedding.

[
72
]

The general rule is that debts
brought into the marriage should be exempt from matrimonial property, just as
are assets brought into the marriage. There is no principled reason to depart
from the rule in this case.

[
73
]

At the date of marriage, the wife
owed $2,895.00 on her Classic Visa and owed $224.00 at the date of the
separation. After the separation, she obtained a RBC Gold Preferred Visa which
had a balance of $5,832.00 as of May 11, 2007 which was the most current
information she had at trial. She also had a Student Loan of $2,699.00 at the
date of the trial.

[
74
]

At the date of marriage, the
husband had a line of credit that was in his name in the amount of $11,354.00.
The line of credit was paid off entirely by the husband shortly after the
marriage with the money gifts from the wedding.

[
75
]

I find that the husband was not
entitled to use that money for the purpose of paying a debt that he had
incurred before the marriage. I find the amount of those money marriage gifts
to be $14,000.00. The husband must pay it back into the assets of the marriage
for distribution. Given that the husband was not entitled to use the funds to
pay his debts incurred before the marriage, I find that he brought into the
marriage a debt of $11,354.00 for which he is responsible personally.

[
76
]

The line of credit at the date of
separation was $13,446.00 and $18,280.00 at the date of the trial. Given that
the debt at the date of marriage was $11,354.00, the amount of the debt that
could be matrimonial debt is $2,092.00 at the date of separation or $6,926.00
at the date of the trial.

[
77
]

As he testified, he may have used
the line of credit among other things to pay for wedding supplies. From my
review of the line or credit, he was paying it off regularly during the
marriage, so if he was buying wedding supplies, the value will be found in
those supplies at the date of separation.  He has not used the line of credit
to purchase supplies since the separation.

[
78
]

The husband also had an RBC Visa
Gold and a CIBC Visa at the date of marriage.

[
79
]

The RBC Visa Gold had a balance at
the date of marriage of $634.51 for which the husband is responsible. At the
date of separation the husband's RBC Visa had a balance of $9,691.48. Therefore
the debt accrued on that card at the date of separation is $9,056.97. At trial
the balance was $9,886.00. Up to trial the accrual of that debt was $9,251.49.

[
80
]

The husband says in his argument
that the RBC Visa was used for the purchase of the wedding materials for the
business. However, he also said at trial that he used that Visa to pay his
parents $10,000.00 during the marriage to repay them. He also explained in his
evidence that his mother had helped him with the down payment for the house.  I
also note that at another point in the trial he said that the $10,000.00 was
used to pay down the line of credit and the documentary evidence supports this.

[
81
]

On my review of the statements
associated with that card I found that during the marriage, in December, 2005,
the husband used that card to pay $10,000.00 on his line of credit. He then
paid off on the card. Further, I found that the major amount he owes on that
Visa account as at trial is for two cheques for $9,900.00 in total on the
account made July 27, 2006, and August 18, 2006, after the separation. There is
no explanation for those cheques.

[
82
]

With respect to the CIBC Visa, on
June 28, 2005, days before the wedding, the husband owed $991.20 on this card.
As at July 27, 2005, the amount owed included $7,953.00. I was not given the
amount actually owing at the date of the marriage. On that card between June 28
and July 27, 2005, he had incurred $21,887.00 in purchases and he had paid
during that period $14,000.00 in total on June 30 and July 5, 2005. My review
of the charges reveals that the charges up to July 27, 2005, were mostly for
the wedding hotel and airfare and car rentals. As at April 2, 2006, the date of
separation, his CIBC Visa balance was about $1,250.00. As of the date of trial,
the balance was $9,498.94. The large increase in his CIBC Visa is entirely due
to his personal expenses since the separation. I have found that there was
$1,250.00 which was attributable as matrimonial debt. That is to be shared by
both parties as matrimonial debt.

[
83
]

In summary, I find that the
husband was responsible for the costs of the wedding and that those costs are
not matrimonial debt.

2.

What are the exemptions?

[
84
]

Property acquired before a
marriage is exempt from distribution as matrimonial property:
S. 7(2)

Matrimonial
Property Act
.

[
85
]

Given that the husband bought the
house before the marriage, any increase in value of the house by the time of
the marriage is exempt from matrimonial property. As discussed above this is
$25,765.00.

[
86
]

The wife was driving the same car
when she got married as she was when they separated and at the date of trial.
That is exempt.

[
87
]

The stock options had decreased in
value, so the husband is entitled to those entirely.

[
88
]

Both parties had RRSPs when they
married and the amounts in their RRSPs at the time of the marriage are exempt.
That amounts to  $5,425.00 for the husband, and $852.00 for the wife.

[
89
]

As to Y & S Wedding Decor,
this company was formed contemporaneously with the marriage and was formed by
both of them. Therefore, there are no exemptions associated with the company.
However, the husband claims that some of the debt that he brought into the
marriage is really debt associated with buying materials for the company which
materials were used by the couple for their wedding. The only evidence that has
been provided suggests that the husband spent $8,500.00 on wedding materials
that were subsequently put into the company. This was not disputed by the wife.
Therefore, I find that the value of the materials put into the company by the
husband is $8,500.00 which is included in the value of the business as
$29,000.00. The balance of the wedding costs are his according to the custom.
Therefore I deduct $8,500.00 from the value of the business leaving $20,500.00
to be included in the matrimonial property for division as set out below. Also,
any debts associated with the business are included in the matrimonial debt.

[
90
]

The amount of the settlement to
the wife for an accident is exempt as to the $10,000.00 that she paid her
mother. The other $3,000.00 appears to have been spent by the wife during the
currency of the marriage on paying her credit card debt. Given that it is not
clear if that debt was incurred during the marriage or before, I find that the
$3,000.00 was mixed into matrimonial property and is not exempt.

[
91
]

As to the wife's debt, at the time
of the marriage, the wife owed $2,895.00 on her credit card. At the date of
separation she owed $224.00. I find that the $224.00 is included in the exempt
debt at the time of the marriage.

[
92
]

For the husband, his line of
credit increased by $2,092.00 during the marriage. The balance of the line of
credit is his responsibility as he brought $11,354.00 into the marriage which
is his debt and I do not allow his use of the wedding gifts to pay down that
debt. At the date of marriage, the husband
’
s
RBC Visa had a balance of $634.51 which is his.

3.

How should the property be divided?

a)       Division
of Matrimonial Property under s. 7(3)

[
93
]

Matrimonial property to be divided
under
s. 7(3)
of the
Matrimonial Property Act
is property that came into
the marriage as a result of being purchased before the marriage which property
has accrued during the marriage. There is no presumption of equal division. The
matrimonial property is to be divided in a manner that is considered just and
equitable by the court: s. 7(3) of the Act taking into account factors set out
in s. 8 of the Act.

[
94
]

The husband argues for an unequal
division.

[
95
]

Given that this was a very short
marriage, there are few of the factors in section 8 that must be considered in
this case. They include: the duration of the marriage; the income, earning
capacity, liabilities, obligations, property and other financial resources of
each spouse during the marriage; the contributions to the company made by each
of them; and any fact or circumstance that is relevant. The property that must
be divided under s. 7(3) is principally the house and the RRSPs.

i)        The
house

[
96
]

The husband argues that the wife
should get no more than 25% of the appreciation in the value of the house. She
argues that she should get half of the appreciation in the value of the house
to the date of the trial:
Hodgson
,
supra
.

[
97
]

During the marriage, the husband
appears to have made significantly more of a financial contribution to the
house than did the wife. In fact, there was no evidence that the wife
contributed directly financially to the house during the marriage.  She did
contribute to other expenses of the marriage. The husband also made more money
during the marriage, and the parties knew this going into the marriage.
Relative uneven income during a marriage is not uncommon and is not usually
considered a factor to justify an uneven distribution. The wife testified that
she and her husband went house hunting together before the wedding, that she
had input into the choices of tile and counter tops, that she contributed to
household finances by buying groceries and household items, and on one occasion
signed over her entire pay cheque to her husband. I accept her evidence in this
regard. Throughout the marriage, the husband had a considerably higher income
than she did. Further, the increase in the value of the house is the result of
market conditions, not the labour of one of the parties. The wife submits that
it is simply a matter of good fortune that her husband and she should share in
equally:
S.W. v. J.W.
,
2005 ABQB 728
,
26 R.F.L. (6th) 168
(at
para.
113
).

[
98
]

The husband argues that the large
increase in the value of the house should be given to him as the house was an
investment made by him and his mother prior to the wedding. The matrimonial
home was purchased by the husband in November, 2004, seven months before the
wedding and after the engagement and he took possession a month before the
wedding. He made a down payment which came from his RRSPs and from his parents.
The wife's name does not appear on title or on the mortgage. Although the
husband says he bought the house as an investment with his mother, the mother's
name does not appear on the title, nor on the loan, nor is  there any evidence
his mother bought the home for an investment. There was little improvement done
to the house after the husband took possession and during the marriage except
some fencing. There is little doubt from the evidence that the wife moved to
Edmonton to make the house her marital home.

[
99
]

In
Wright‑Watts v.
Watts
,
supra
, McMahon J. awarded the wife 25% of the increase in
value of the properties owned by the husband before the marriage including
rental properties, taking into account the fact that the marriage was short and
that the husband had a greater income.
In
Wallat v. Marshall

2005
ABQB 426
Coutu J. awarded the husband 30% of the increased value of the
property brought into the marriage by the wife taking into account his
$12,000.00 financial contribution to the property, his non‑financial
contributions to the marriage, and the length of the marriage.

[
100
]

The house in the case before me
was the matrimonial home. The wife had to move from Calgary without employment
and make a fresh start in Edmonton. When the wife moved into the home two
months after the wedding, the house was their home until the separation. I note
that the increase in the value of the home up until the separation and to the
date of trial was almost entirely due to the hot real estate market in Edmonton
and little was due to anything either of the parties did to the home.
Therefore, the equity should be divided equally unless there are factors that
would suggest otherwise. I do not divide the equity in the home equally.

[
101
]

The amount of the mortgage at the
date of marriage was $239,235.00 and at the date of separation was $238,988.00.
At the date of the trial it was $223,235.00. Between the date of the marriage
and the date of separation, the mortgage decreased only slightly
–
$247.00, but the mortgage at the date of trial had
decreased by $16,000.00. The husband was solely responsible for the decrease in
the mortgage amount between the separation and the trial. After the separation
the equity increased in the house due in part to mortgage payments made by the
husband.
Those payments were all made by the husband,
without any contribution by the wife. Since the separation, the husband has
lived in the home and paid the mortgage and maintained the home. He continues
to live in the house. She has gone back to Calgary and made a home for herself
there.

ii)       RRSPs

[
102
]

Over the marriage and to the date
of trial, the husband's RRSPs increased in value by $4,966.99; the wife's by
$188.00 for a total increase of $5,54.99. As with the house, the wife had
little in her RRSPs at the date of the marriage and the bulk of the increase
was due to the larger amount of RRSPs brought into the marriage by the husband.

iii)      Conclusion
for division of property under s. 7(3)

[
103
]

In looking at this marriage, which
was of short duration ‑ 9 months, I find that it would be unfair to
divide the property in the marriage as at the date of the trial. They left the
marriage in April, 2006 and it was over. The trial was held in September, 2007,
that is, about 15 months after the separation. That period of time was longer
than the marriage itself. During the separation, the parties lived completely
separate lives, earning incomes and going into debt as they individually saw
fit. The husband continued to make all payments for the house including
maintenance, utilities, taxes and insurance. He lived in the house for that
period of time and continues to do so.

[
104
]

Given the short marriage and the
complete separation of all financial matters after that short marriage, there
is nothing to suggest that the parties should share in the equity of the house
up until the day of trial.

[
105
]

The house gained $47,000.00
($265,000.00 ‑ $312,000.00) in value during the marriage. I have not
taken into account the increase due to payments on the mortgage, given that
very little of the principle was being paid over that short time. I was not
given the amount of the mortgage at the date of the marriage in any event.

[
106
]

I am dividing equally the increase
in the house during the marriage. The wife should not share in the fortuitous
increase in value of the home from the date of separation, having done nothing
to increase that value. The husband is entitled to all of the increase in the
value of the home since the separation.

[
107
]

The RRSPs gained $5,155.00 until
the date of the trial. The wife argues that the increase in the value of the
RRSPs from the date of the marriage to the date of trial should be divided
equally between them. There was no evidence that either party made contributions
after separation or that the increase in value was due to specific efforts. The
husband submits that since neither party had any involvement or contribution to
the acquisition, retention or growth of the other parties' investments, each
should retain 100% of the increase in their own RRSPs. I agree with the wife.
With respect to the very small increase in value of the RRSPs, it is only
reasonable that each party retain its RRSP but the increase in value over the
marriage to trial be shared equally between the parties.

[
108
]

In summary, the matrimonial
property to be divided under s. 7(4) is as follows:

the house                       $47,000.00

the RRSPs                      $5,155.00

Total                             $52,155.00

b)       Division
of Matrimonial Property under s. 7(4)

[
109
]

The property to be divided under
s. 7(4) includes the household furnishings, the company, the money wedding
gifts and the debt. The
Matrimonial Property Act
s. 7(4) contemplates
that this matrimonial property should be divided equally.

i)        Household
furnishings

[
110
]

The household furnishings worth
$3,000.00 are to be shared equally.

ii)       The
Company

[
111
]

With respect to the company, Y
& S Wedding Decor, the equity in the goods still retained by the husband is
$20,500.00 which is matrimonial property to be divided equally. The
equalization payment is $10,250.00 and the husband may do what he wishes with
the material.

iii)      Debt

[
112
]

Neither the wife nor the husband
should have to share in the debts that the other accrued prior to the marriage.
Nor, given the factors set out above, should either be responsible for the debt
accrued after the separation.

[
113
]

There is, however, matrimonial
debt to be shared which was accrued during the marriage.

[
114
]

The wife's debt decreased during
the marriage. At the date of marriage, the wife owed $2,895.00 on her Classic
Visa and owed $224.00 at the date of the separation. Matrimonial assets and/or
her damages payment of $3,000.00 were used to pay down her debt in the amount
of $2,671.00. The $224.00 left on the card at the date of separation is
attributable to the debt that she owed at the date of the marriage and will not
be shared by the parties.

[
115
]

The husband had a debt of
$2,092.00 in his line of credit at separation which the wife must share.
Finally, I am attributing $1,250.00 from his CIBC Visa as matrimonial debt
which must be divided between the parties equally.

[
116
]

The total debt of the husband to
be shared is $3,342.00.

iv)      Wedding
gifts

[
117
]

Now I turn to the wedding gifts.
The only one at issue is the cash. The husband was not entitled to use that
money to pay for the wedding. Therefore, I am treating the $14,000.00 as though
it is in a cash account for the benefit of both the husband and wife, that is
as cash to be distributed as matrimonial property. When people gave the money,
they gave it to both of them and it became matrimonial property. When it was
not used to buy things for the home, it remained cash.

[
118
]

In summary, the matrimonial
property to be divided under
s. 7(4)
is as follows:

Household goods                                    $3,000.00

Y & S Wedding Decor                             $20,500.00

Wedding gifts                                         $14,000.00

Matrimonial debt                                    ($3,342.00)

Total                                                     $34,158.00

v)       Conclusion

[
119
]

The total of the matrimonial
property to be divided is $37,500.00. The debt to be divided is $3,342.00.
Therefore, the equity to be divided equally between the parties is $34,158.00.

Conclusion

[
120
]

I find that the  Mahr is not an
enforceable contract. I do not have to conclude that it is not enforceable by
virtue of uncertainty. It is unenforceable because it does not comply with the
requirements of
s. 38
of the
Matrimonial Property Act
. Therefore, I have
divided the matrimonial property in accordance with the Act taking into
consideration the factors set out in
s. 7
and s. 8.

[
121
]

This was a short marriage and for
the reasons set out above, I have not included the accrual in value of the
property brought into the marriage by the husband. Further, I have found that
the accrual of property and debts after the separation would not be just or
equitable.

[
122
]

I find that the accrued value of
the house during the marriage is $47,000.00 which is to be divided equally
between the parties. The accrual of the RRSPs for $5,155.00 is to be divided
equally. The balance of the matrimonial property and debt amounts to $34,158.00
which is to be divided equally. The total property to be divided is $52,155.00
under
s. 7(3)
of the
Matrimonial Property Act
and $34,158.00 which is to
be divided under s. 7(4) of the Act for a total of $86,313.00.  The
equalization payment to be made to the wife by the husband is $43,156.00.

[
123
]

The husband keeps the house, his
RRSPs and the materials in the company. The wife keeps her RRSPs and gets the
equalization payment.

[
124
]

The parties may address costs if
they arrange to do so with me within 30 days of the release of this judgment.
If they fail to do so, the wife is awarded costs under the appropriate column.
